clinical_category: Osteoporosis - lifestyle measures that complement treatment
blueprint_topic: Health-maintenance behaviors that support bone health and fracture prevention
stem: A client newly diagnosed with osteoporosis says, "Now that I have medication, diet and lifestyle no longer matter." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Medication may reduce fracture risk, but lifestyle measures still matter: maintain adequate calcium and vitamin D intake, avoid smoking, limit excessive alcohol, remain safely active, and take prescribed osteoporosis therapy as directed.
options.B: That is correct; once osteoporosis medication is started, calcium, vitamin D, smoking, alcohol use, and physical activity no longer influence bone or fall health.
options.C: Stop the prescribed medication and rely only on supplements and lifestyle changes because these measures replace pharmacologic treatment in established osteoporosis.
options.D: Avoid all physical activity to protect the skeleton because inactivity is the preferred long-term strategy after osteoporosis is diagnosed.

rationale: A is correct. Current NIAMS guidance describes osteoporosis management as a combination of appropriate medication when prescribed, adequate calcium and vitamin D, healthy nutrition, safe physical activity, fall prevention, smoking cessation, and moderation of alcohol. NIAMS specifically notes that calcium, vitamin D, exercise, and other healthy lifestyle measures remain important even when osteoporosis medication is used. B incorrectly treats drug therapy as a substitute for all other risk-reduction measures. C improperly substitutes lifestyle measures for indicated pharmacologic therapy. D promotes inactivity, which can worsen muscle weakness, balance, and fall risk. The final item is intentionally distinct from V2-Q1895: Q1895 tests exercise-program selection, whereas this item tests the relationship between lifestyle measures and prescribed osteoporosis treatment.
educational_objective: Teach that osteoporosis medication and lifestyle measures are complementary: adequate calcium/vitamin D, smoking cessation, moderation of alcohol, safe activity, fall prevention, and adherence to prescribed therapy all remain relevant.
source_organization: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Osteoporosis: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take; Osteoporosis Causes, Risk Factors, & Symptoms
source_locator: NIAMS osteoporosis guidance → Treatment/Steps to Take: even when osteoporosis medications are prescribed, recommended calcium and vitamin D intake, exercise, fall prevention and other healthy lifestyle measures remain important. Lifestyle/Risk Factors: smoking and chronic heavy alcohol use increase osteoporosis/fracture risk; diet low in calcium/vitamin D contributes to bone loss.
source_claim_supported: Current NIAMS guidance directly supports combining medication, adequate calcium/vitamin D, safe activity, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation and fall prevention rather than treating any one component as a complete replacement for the others.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: provide preventive-health education, support healthy lifestyle choices and adherence to long-term health-maintenance plans, and reduce modifiable risk factors for chronic disease and injury.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's generic lifestyle list to prevent semantic duplication with V2-Q1895. The final item tests whether lifestyle measures remain necessary alongside prescribed osteoporosis medication and explicitly avoids both medication-only and lifestyle-only false dichotomies.
audit_findings: The source's lifestyle list overlapped with the preceding exercise-prevention item and required differentiation.
Fresh NIAMS review directly supports calcium/vitamin D, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, safe activity and medication adherence as complementary osteoporosis-management measures.
The final item avoids suggesting that lifestyle alone replaces indicated medication or that medication makes lifestyle irrelevant.
Distractors test medication-only care, lifestyle-only substitution and harmful inactivity; none is defensible.
